questions.q: What's the key gap between a working demo on your laptop and a finished portfolio project, according to this lesson?
options: Documentation and a few finishing touches -- a clear README, run instructions, and stated limitations
A working demo is already a complete portfolio project with nothing left to do
Rewriting the entire project in a different programming language
Removing all mention of any tradeoffs or design decisions
questions.explain: The gap is mainly documentation and polish -- a README covering the problem, architecture, tradeoffs, run instructions, and known limitations -- not a rewrite of the working project itself.

questions.q: Why should a README explicitly state known limitations (like 'fixed-price only, no auctions')?
options: Limitations should always be hidden from reviewers
It's required by GitHub's terms of service
Being upfront about scope reads as engineering maturity, not as a weakness, and matches the deliberate scope set in the kickoff lesson
It has no effect on how a reviewer perceives the project
questions.explain: Stating limitations plainly signals that the scope was a deliberate engineering decision (as set in Lesson 8), not an oversight -- which reads as maturity to a reviewer or interviewer.

questions.q: If an interviewer asks 'why approval instead of escrow for this marketplace,' what's the strongest answer?
options: 'I don't remember why I chose that'
'Escrow and approval are exactly the same thing'
'It was the only option available in Solidity'

'The seller keeps control of the NFT until it actually sells, matching how production marketplaces like Seaport work -- the tradeoff is buyItem has to re-verify ownership and approval at purchase time'
questions.explain: A strong answer names the actual design decision, why it was made, and the tradeoff it introduces -- exactly what this lesson calls out as the kind of answer that demonstrates real engineering judgment.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does an indexer matter enough to be one of the three expected interview questions about this project?
options: Because a node's RPC interface can't answer an aggregate question like 'show me every active listing' -- the indexer is what makes that possible
Indexers are legally required for all NFT marketplaces
An indexer replaces the smart contract entirely
Indexers only matter for DeFi protocols, not NFT marketplaces
questions.explain: This echoes Lesson 10's core point: a node can't answer aggregate queries about contract state, so the indexer is what turns raw events into something a frontend (and an interviewer) can meaningfully ask about.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is generally more valuable in a portfolio than a long list of projects?
options: A small number of complete, well-documented projects with answers ready for their specific tradeoffs
The total number of GitHub repositories, regardless of completeness
Having every project written in a different blockchain framework
Avoiding any discussion of tradeoffs to appear more confident
questions.explain: This closes the loop with the point made back in Chapter 1: depth over breadth -- a few fully-finished, well-documented projects demonstrate real engineering ability better than many shallow ones.
